body.text: Over the past decade, the Asia-Pacific region has become a global leader in digital asset adoption. Broadly defined as the representation of resources and other instruments that are issued and transferred using blockchain technology, a number of Asia-Pacific financial institutions have made big investments on this new wave of financial technology. Surveys have indicated that 62 percent of Asia-Pacific institutions have already committed capital to digital asset infrastructure, compared to 27 percent in North America. The amount of resources deployed to build out digital asset offerings is significant, with nearly eight in 10 Asia-Pacific institutions allocating more than $1 million. The result is that the Asia-Pacific just recorded the world’s fastest regional growth in blockchain-based crypto-asset transactions, expanding by 69 percent between mid-2024 and mid-2025, according to the OECD’s 2026 Asia Capital Markets Report.

The types of digital assets offered by Asia-Pacific financial institutions extend far beyond cryptocurrency. In April 2026, Singaporean bank OCBC and its asset management arm, Lion Global Investors, partnered with the digital asset exchange DigiFT, to issue the OCBC-LionGlobal Physical Gold Fund Token (“GOLDX token”). This token claims to be Southeast Asia’s first tokenized physical gold fund available on a public blockchain and allows institutional and corporate investors to own physical gold with the liquidity and verification benefits of blockchain technology. In 2026, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) granted two stablecoin licenses to HSBC and a joint venture backed by Standard Chartered Hong Kong, facilitating easier trade in traditionally illiquid assets. Japan’s largest bank, Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking (MUFG) recently launched Progmat, a digital asset infrastructure for issuing and managing security tokens, which represent traditional financial assets like bonds, real estate, or corporate shares. Progmat is now backed by other large Japanese financial institutions, such as Mizuho, the Tokyo Stock Exchange and SBI Group.

However, these sophisticated digital assets are the result of complex and constantly evolving regulatory regimes that differ significantly from each other. Hong Kong’s recently finalized regulations on Virtual Asset Trading Platforms (VATP) are particularly comprehensive, covering service providers under distinct licensing categories, mirroring traditional securities rules. Singapore regulates cryptocurrency through a tailored, activity-based approach rather than a single framework. The Payment Services Act covers e-money or digital payment tokens and the Securities and Futures Act governs digital assets resembling securities. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) emphasizes consumer protection via mandatory customer asset segregation, statutory trusts, and licensing thresholds. Japan runs one of the world’s most sophisticated and onerous digital asset regimes, featuring granular legal categories (Crypto Assets, stablecoins, and security tokens) each under tailored oversight, paired with strict investor protections like mandatory cold-wallet segregation. Recent reforms in July 2026 signal a friendlier trajectory, reclassifying crypto as financial instruments under the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act, cutting taxes to a flat 20 percent, and aligning treatment with stocks to attract institutional investors.
